== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' was born about 1776. The GRONI civil-death index records a James Glasgow aged 90 dying on 14 December 1866 in the Cookstown registration district, matching this profile's earlier year-only death source and approximate birth year.<ref name="GRONI1866">[https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death General Register Office for Northern Ireland, civil death index], James Glasgow, died 14 December 1866, age 90, Cookstown registration district, D/1866/99/1009/2/195. The registration district does not establish an exact death address; the full return has not been viewed.</ref> His birth year is approximate.

At present, little else can be stated securely about his life. A number of earlier probate records for men named James Glasgow survive in County Tyrone and neighbouring County Londonderry. Several occur in or near the Cookstown area, but none has yet been proved to refer to this James Glasgow.

=== Same-name probate records ===

The following records are relevant to research into James Glasgow families in the Cookstown district and surrounding area. They are listed here as comparison records only.

* '''1794 — Drummon, County Tyrone.''' A James Glasgow appears in the PRONI pre-1858 wills and administrations index with a residence recorded as Drummon. Drummond in the Derryloran/Cookstown locality is a possible modern identification, but this remains provisional.<ref name="PRONI1794">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Pre-1858 Wills and Admons: James Glasgow, Drummond, County Tyrone, 19 December 1794].</ref>

* '''1807 — Drumcarn, County Tyrone.''' A James Glasgow is recorded with a residence at Drumcarn. The historical place-name has not yet been securely matched to a modern townland.<ref name="PRONI1807">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Pre-1858 Wills and Admons: James Glasgow, Drumcarn, County Tyrone, 1807].</ref>

* '''1820 — Drumeen, County Londonderry.''' A James Glasgow is recorded at Drumeen. The county designation suggests Drummeen townland near Moneymore.<ref name="PRONI1820">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Pre-1858 Wills and Admons: James Glasgow, Drumeen, County Londonderry, 1820].</ref>

* '''1822 — Drumeen.''' James Glasgow, described as a '''farmer''', appears in an Armagh Diocesan Administration Bond at Drumeen.<ref name="PRONI1822">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Armagh Diocesan Administration Bonds: James Glasgow, farmer, Drumeen, 1822].</ref> The locality may be the same Drummeen represented by the 1820 entry, but whether the two records concern the same man is unproved.

* '''1826 — Oritor.''' James Glasgow, described as a '''gentleman''', appears in an Armagh Diocesan Administration Bond at Oritor, County Tyrone.<ref name="PRONI1826">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Armagh Diocesan Administration Bonds: James Glasgow, gentleman, Oritor, 1826].</ref> Oritor forms part of a recurring cluster of Glasgow records west of Cookstown.

* '''1831 — Cookstown, County Tyrone.''' The PRONI wills and administrations index entry for James Glasgow of Cookstown in 1831 is assigned to [[Glasgow-4024|James Glasgow (about 1791–before 13 March 1831)]]. St Luran's register records that man, resident at Cookstown, buried on 13 March 1831 aged 40.<ref name="PRONI1831">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Pre-1858 Wills and Admons: James Glasgow, Cookstown, County Tyrone, 1831]. The item-level transcription should be re-verified.</ref><ref name="StLuran1831">[https://www.cotyroneireland.com/churchrecord/saintluran1830-1849.html Derryloran Parish, St Luran's burial register transcript], James Glasgow, Cookstown, buried 13 March 1831, age 40.</ref> It is excluded from this profile.

* '''1836 — Killycarragh/Killycurragh, County Tyrone.''' A James Glasgow is recorded at Killycarragh.<ref name="PRONI1836">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Names, Pre-1858 Wills and Admons: James Glasgow, Killycarragh, 1836].</ref> The place is provisionally identified with Killycurragh in the Oritor/Derryloran locality, close to the other Cookstown-area occurrences.

Taken together, these records show that several men named James Glasgow were present in the wider Cookstown–Moneymore area during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. They should not be combined into a single biography without further evidence.

== Research Notes ==
The profile birth year of '''about 1776''' is uncertain. It should not be derived from the 1794 probate entry unless that record can first be shown to concern this James Glasgow.

The earlier probate records may represent several different men. In particular, differences in residence, date and descriptions such as '''farmer''' and '''gentleman''' should be treated as evidence requiring reconciliation rather than assumed variations in one man's record.

No parent, spouse or child should be attached to this profile unless a source explicitly identifies the relationship.

Possible connections to [[Glasgow-1970|James Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-2988|James Glasgow]] or other earlier Glasgow families remain unproved.

=== Distinct 1831 Cookstown burial ===

[[Glasgow-4024|James Glasgow of Cookstown (abt.1791-bef.1831)]] was buried at St Luran's on 13 March 1831 aged 40. He has a separate profile because his age is incompatible with this profile's reported 1776–1866 lifespan. The burial is not evidence for this profile's death.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast Juvenile Society secretary, 1830–1831. James Glasgow and Walter Moffat are named secretaries announcing the Belfast Juvenile Society’s sixth annual meeting at Rev. Dr Cooke’s May Street meeting-house on Monday 15 November 1830. In March 1831 Rev. Walter Moffatt and Mr James Glasgow attended a Knockbracken meeting as the Society’s deputation; Rev. Thomas Houston chaired it.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 12 November 1830, p.2, Belfast Juvenile Society sixth annual meeting announcement; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390573239/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 4 March 1831, p.4, Belfast Juvenile Society, Knockbracken meeting; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390543442/ record].</ref> The repeated society and associates support one society account. The same Walter Moffat appears in the 1828 Institution report, making [[Glasgow-1780]] a compatible student/ministry-network candidate; this does not prove that the society secretary is the college student. The newspaper does not call James the president, chair or minister. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast tobacco seller, 1822–23. James Glasgow offered leaf tobacco in three Belfast advertisements in 1822–23. The August 1822 notice directs buyers to him at James M’Master’s; the May 1823 notice locates samples at M’Master’s North Street premises.<ref>The Irishman, 15 March 1822, p. 2, tobacco advertisement dated 9 March; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61259036/ record]; The Irishman, 23 August 1822, p. 3, tobacco advertisement dated 20 August; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61260054/ record]; The Irishman, 30 May 1823, p. 3, tobacco advertisement dated 27 May; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61261904/ record].</ref> Repeated name, trade and contact support a consolidated seller account. M’Master’s premises are a commercial contact, not a proved home or owned property. No age, family or link to William Glasgow the grocer is stated. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast tobacco seller, 1822–23. An auction notice describes the large shop and stores at No.32 Rosemary Street, Belfast, as formerly occupied by Mr James Glasgow. The lease interest was offered for sale on 1 April 1828; the notice dated 21 March gives 34 years unexpired from 1 November next and £30 late Irish currency yearly rent.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 1 April 1828, p.3, auction of shop and stores, No.32 Rosemary Street; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390544933/ record].</ref> Former occupancy is explicit; ownership, trade and residence are not. The surname is certain, but identity with the 1822–23 tobacco seller, William the grocer or another James remains unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, plaintiff in Dublin Exchequer, 1820. James Glasgow was plaintiff against Maxwell Lepper and Clotworthy Dobbin in a Court of Exchequer report headed Dublin, 22 June 1820. The defendants’ motion to rescind the contempt process was refused with costs and liberty for the plaintiff to continue process.<ref>The Irishman, 30 June 1820, p. 2, Court of Exchequer, Dublin, 22 June; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61258711/ record].</ref> The report gives a procedural decision, not final judgment on the dispute, and no age, occupation, residence or relatives for James. George Frederick Moulds is named as plaintiff’s agent. Identity with the later Belfast tobacco seller or any candidate is unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, plaintiff in Dublin Exchequer, 1820. A separate report lists James Glasgow on the petty jury for Friday 1 August 1828. He is a juror, not one of the accused in the following riot-and-assault report.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 5 August 1828, p.4, petty jury, Friday 1 August; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390549197/ record].</ref> The name is James Glasgow, not the automated index’s combined William James Glasgow. No residence, occupation or kin is stated. This remains an unassigned legal occurrence; identity with the 1820 Exchequer plaintiff is unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, plaintiff in Dublin Exchequer, 1820. A report in the Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser states that the parties in cause and cross-cause included Robert Thompson of Newry, the Rev. Mr Walsh of Ballymena, and Mr Barbour of Lisburn; it then says “The following were the Jury” and lists James Glasgow.<ref>Freeman's Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 3 November 1823, p. 3, trial report and jury list; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050060364/ record].</ref> The original page confirms James Glasgow’s jury role in this reported trial. The newspaper issue is from Dublin, but the inspected passage does not show a court heading or venue. Newry, Ballymena and Lisburn describe other named parties, not the juror. The occurrence is compatible with, but not proved to be the same person as, the James Glasgow on the 1828 Belfast petty jury; identity with the 1820 Exchequer plaintiff is also unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

=== James Glasgow, Cookstown tea agent, 1849 ===

Eleven inspected issues from 23 June to 25 October 1849 name James Glasgow, merchant at Cookstown, in John Cassell’s agent lists, including five-shilling tea. Repeated advertisements document a trading role, not eleven people or independent family proofs. No age, relatives or street address is supplied; the separately named John Glasgow agency remains distinct.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1256974996/ The Sligo Champion, 1849-06-23, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1256975013/ The Sligo Champion, 1849-06-30, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100143/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-08-23, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100155/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-08-30, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100180/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-09-13, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100191/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-09-20, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100202/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-09-27, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100214/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-10-04, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100225/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-10-11, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100236/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-10-18, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1369100248/ The Fermanagh Mail, and Enniskillen Chronicle, 1849-10-25, p. 1, Cookstown James Glasgow agent-list entry].</ref>

The Cookstown chronology supports this as a possible identity. [[Glasgow-3196|James Glasgow]] remains an alternative: his description as farmer in his son’s 1859 marriage does not exclude earlier trading. The advertisements identify neither household, and repeated notices do not establish a relationship to the separately named John Glasgow.
